title: BYOK cost accounting is wrong by 10-60x for unknown models; OpenRouter has no pricing table and Anthropic's default contradicts its own table
impact: Per-user spend shown in the BYOK UI and platform-wide spend on the admin health endpoint are materially wrong — a cheap model can be reported at 60x its real price and an expensive OpenRouter model at a fraction of it. Any budgeting or alerting built on these numbers is unusable.
fix: Make unknown models explicit: return None/0 with a `pricing_unknown` flag instead of silently using a wrong default, fix the Anthropic capabilities default to match its own Haiku entry, and add a real per-model table (or fetch OpenRouter's /models pricing) for OpenRouter.
corr: OpenRouterProvider defines no MODEL_PRICING, so all its models (7B Mistral through Claude Opus) are costed at the flat capabilities default 0.005/0.015, which is off by up to ~100x for cheap models; both OpenAI and Anthropic MODEL_PRICING tables also only cover 2024-era ids, so newer models fall back to a default (OpenAI 0.01/0.03, Anthropic 0.0025/0.0125 — the latter is actually within ~20% of current Claude pricing). This affects only the `cost_usd` value passed to `record_llm_call` (Prometheus) and the admin-only `/byok/system/health` `total_cost`. It is NOT a "same model priced 10x apart" bug — `claude-3-haiku*` always hits the table; the contradicting `get_capabilities()` value is stale informational metadata only. And it is not the reason BYOK spend numbers are unusable: `usage_stats` is in-memory and is reset to zero by `load_user_providers`/`update_provider_in_service` on every `/byok/generate` call, and no frontend surface consumes `/byok/usage-stats` or `/byok/generate` at all. Severity: low (metric/telemetry accuracy and stale pricing tables), not medium.
evidence: `get_model_pricing` falls back to `get_capabilities()` defaults for any model not in `MODEL_PRICING`. AnthropicProvider.MODEL_PRICING has `"claude-3-haiku": (0.00025, 0.00125)` while its own `get_capabilities()` returns `cost_per_1k_input_tokens=0.0025, cost_per_1k_output_tokens=0.0125` annotated `# Claude 3 Haiku pricing` — the same model priced 10x apart depending on the code path. `OpenRouterProvider` declares no MODEL_PRICING at all, so every one of its models (from 7B Mistral to Claude Opus) is costed at the flat `0.005/0.015` "Average pricing" default. Both tables only contain 2024-era ids (gpt-4-turbo/gpt-4o, claude-3.x); anything newer prefix-matches nothing and is billed at the OpenAI default `0.01/0.03`. These numbers feed `update_usage_stats` → `record_llm_call(..., cost_usd=response.cost)` and the `/byok/usage-stats` and admin `/byok/system/health` `total_cost` figures.
repro: POST /byok/generate with provider=openrouter, model="mistralai/mistral-7b-instruct" → response.cost computed at 0.005/0.015 per 1k. Or model="gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18"… any id not prefix-matching the table → 0.01/0.03.

title: Anthropic key validation hardcodes a single Claude 3 model id, so valid keys can be rejected outright
impact: If a key lacks access to that one 2024 snapshot (or the snapshot is retired), `/byok/validate` and `POST /byok/api-keys` report "API key validation failed with provider" and the user cannot register a perfectly good Anthropic key at all. Users who do get in are shown a model dropdown containing only retired/legacy Claude 3 ids.
fix: Validate with an auth-only endpoint (GET https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models) as the other two providers do, and refresh get_available_models from that response instead of a hardcoded 2024 list.
corr: Core issue confirmed but severity is low, not medium, and the framing should shift. AnthropicProvider.validate_api_key (llm_provider_service.py:314-332) is the only provider still validating by posting a live completion against a hardcoded model id, after OpenAI (:196-205) and OpenRouter (:405-413) were deliberately moved to auth-only /models checks. Consequence: any non-200 from a valid key (rate limit, zero credit balance, workspace model restriction, or future retirement of claude-3-haiku-20240307) is surfaced as "API key validation failed with provider" on POST /byok/api-keys, /byok/validate and /byok/test/{provider}; validation also incurs a billable inference call. It is not true today that ordinary valid Anthropic keys are rejected, since Anthropic keys are not per-model scoped and that snapshot is still live. Separately and more concretely, get_available_models (:346-351) advertises only three early-2024 Claude 3 snapshots (two of which are deprecated) while MODEL_PRICING already prices claude-3-5-*, and that list is rendered as the user's model picker via GET /byok/models/{provider} and /byok/providers. Fix: use Anthropic's GET /v1/models for validation and refresh the model list.
evidence: Anthropic validation posts `{"model": "claude-3-haiku-20240307", "messages":[…], "max_tokens":1}` and returns `response.status_code == 200`. The OpenAI and OpenRouter providers were explicitly changed away from exactly this pattern — their code carries the comment "Validate via the auth-only /models endpoint rather than a chat completion against a hardcoded model — a key scoped to only newer models (no gpt-3.5 access) is still valid." Anthropic still advertises only `claude-3-opus-20240229 / claude-3-sonnet-20240229 / claude-3-haiku-20240307` in get_available_models, even though its own MODEL_PRICING table already lists claude-3-5-sonnet/haiku that the model list omits.
repro: POST /byok/validate {provider:"anthropic", api_key:<valid key without claude-3-haiku-20240307 access>} → {valid:false}.

title: Quick Tailor result is persisted only by the browser — closing the modal loses the tailored resume (and cancels/retries the job)
impact: If the user closes the modal or the tab (the UI only pleads "Don't close this window"), the fork silently remains a byte-identical copy of the parent while the LLM+compile job still runs and is paid for; the tailored content survives only as a hidden checkpoint. Dismissing also trips the cancel-during-streaming path above, producing an extra retried LLM call and a "Tailoring failed" state.
fix: Have the orchestrator write `optimized_latex` to the resume server-side when `resume_id` was supplied (as the quick-tailor/academic-convert flows imply), and treat the frontend save as a no-op refresh.
corr: Core defect confirmed (medium). Two refinements: (1) the tailored content is not lost outright — it is persisted as an auto-save Optimization checkpoint on the fork and is listable/restorable via GET/POST /resumes/{id}/checkpoints, so the correct statement is "the fork's latex_content silently stays a byte-identical copy of the parent, with the tailored text only reachable through the checkpoint history"; (2) the user never observes the "Tailoring failed" state on dismiss because the modal unmounts immediately via onClose — the wasted retry LLM call and terminal job.failed happen invisibly server-side. Fix: have the orchestrator (or a small worker step) write optimized_latex to Resume.latex_content when the job was started with a resume_id created for quick-tailor, and/or stop cancelling on backdrop/Escape dismiss.
evidence: The backend creates the fork with `latex_content=parent.latex_content` and never writes the optimized text back: on success the orchestrator only enqueues `record_auto_save_checkpoint(resume_id, user_id, optimized_latex)`, which inserts an `Optimization` checkpoint row (auto_save_worker.py:137-155) and never touches `Resume.latex_content`; the job.completed payload does not even include `optimized_latex`. Persistence lives entirely in the modal: `if (state.status === 'completed') { … await apiClient.updateResume(forkId, { latex_content: state.streamingLatex }) }`, where streamingLatex is the WebSocket accumulation. Dismissing the modal while running calls `handleCancel()` → `cancel()` → sets the Redis cancel flag.
repro: Start Quick Tailor, close the modal after ~10s, reopen the fork → identical to the parent. Or let it finish with the WebSocket dropped: nothing is saved.

title: Global body-size limit only inspects Content-Length, so chunked uploads reach unbounded file.read()
impact: An unauthenticated-size-limit bypass: a chunked multipart POST streams an arbitrarily large body into memory in the API process. Combined with a crafted DOCX (a 12 MB deflate stream expanding to gigabytes — the parsers apply no decompressed-size guard), a single request can OOM the backend container.
fix: Enforce the ceiling while streaming (count bytes in the ASGI receive loop, reject when the running total exceeds max_bytes) and route every upload handler through `format_routes._read_upload_capped` plus a decompressed-size check before invoking a ZIP-based parser.
corr: The Content-Length-only check in BodySizeLimitMiddleware plus the uncapped `await file.read()` in POST /resumes/builder/seed-upload is a real inconsistency: that handler is the one upload path with neither validate_file_upload() nor the chunked-safe _read_upload_capped() used by format_routes.py, so a chunked (no Content-Length) multipart request skips the 12MB global ceiling. But it is authenticated-only (get_current_user_required) and globally rate-limited, the shipped nginx config caps bodies at 50M including chunked, and starlette spools >1MB multipart file parts to a disk temp file — so the practical effect is a 12MB->50MB limit slip (unbounded only if uvicorn is exposed without the proxy), not an unauthenticated container OOM. The missing decompressed-size guard in the DOCX/PDF parsers is a distinct issue reachable within the 12MB limit regardless of this bypass. Suggested severity: low.
evidence: `BodySizeLimitMiddleware.dispatch` does `content_length = request.headers.get("content-length"); if content_length: ... 413` — with no Content-Length (HTTP/1.1 `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, which httpx/curl will use for a streamed body) the check is skipped entirely. `/resumes/builder/seed-upload` then does `content = await file.read()` with no cap and no `validate_file_upload(file)` call (unlike routes.py:350), handing the bytes to mammoth/python-docx/pdfplumber. Only format_routes.py has a capped reader (`_read_upload_capped`).
repro: curl -X POST http://localhost:8030/resumes/builder/seed-upload -H 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' -F file=@big.docx (no Content-Length header) — middleware does not 413.

title: cleanup_expired_jobs_task marks still-running jobs as failed based on submission time, without revoking them
impact: With `--concurrency=4` and a 10-job Batch Tailor (each combined job can legitimately run up to compile_timeout+180s), the queued tail exceeds 10 minutes of wall-clock since submission and gets a spurious terminal `job.failed`. Because the frontend reducer ignores terminal transitions after the first one (useJobStream.reducer.ts:78-86), those jobs stay "failed" in the UI forever even though the worker later completes them and overwrites the state snapshot.
fix: Use `last_updated` (progress heartbeat) rather than `submitted_at`, only mark failed when no event has been seen for the stall window, skip jobs whose `:result` key exists, and `celery_app.control.revoke(task_id, terminate=True)` when you do declare them dead.
corr: cleanup_expired_jobs_task measures its 10-minute stuck-job threshold from meta_data["submitted_at"] (submission time) rather than from state_data["last_updated"] or job start, so a job that waited in the Celery queue for ~10 minutes and then legitimately began processing can be published as terminal job.failed(error_code="timeout") seconds after it actually started. It also does not check for an existing latexy:job:{id}:result and does not revoke the Celery task, so the job keeps running and later overwrites the state snapshot to "completed" — which REST consumers (GET /jobs/batch/{batch_id}) recover from, but a live WebSocket session does not, because useJobStream.reducer.ts:86-89 ignores terminal events after the first. Contrary to the finding, still-queued jobs (status "queued") are exempt, and no job legitimately processes for over 10 minutes (task time_limit is compile_timeout+180, <=~420s); the only trigger is queue wait being counted as processing time. Combined with the hourly beat cadence and the self-healing snapshot, real-world severity is low-to-medium. Fix: use max(last_updated, started_at) as the baseline, skip jobs that already have a :result key, and revoke the Celery task before publishing the failure.
evidence: `processing_timeout = 10 * 60` … `submitted_at = meta_data.get("submitted_at", ...)`; `if time.time() - submitted_at > processing_timeout: publish_event(job_id_to_check, "job.failed", {"error_code": "timeout", "error_message": "Job timed out — worker may have crashed"})`. The threshold is measured from *submission*, not from `last_updated` (which the same loop already reads), no check is made for an existing `latexy:job:{id}:result`, and the Celery task is never revoked.
repro: Submit a batch of 10 combined jobs on a 4-concurrency worker and wait for the hourly cleanup beat (or call POST /jobs/system/cleanup) — jobs still in the queue >10 min get job.failed.

title: embed_resume_task reuses the module-global async SQLAlchemy engine across per-task asyncio.run() event loops
impact: Resume embeddings (pgvector semantic search / ATS vector features) fail from the second embed task onward in each worker process; the task swallows the error (`except Exception ... return {"success": False}`) after 2 retries and callers are fire-and-forget (resume_routes.py:513, 833, 1049), so the failure is invisible except in logs.
fix: Give embed_resume_task its own per-invocation engine + `await engine.dispose()` in a finally, matching auto_save_worker._do_auto_save, or hold a single long-lived event loop per worker process instead of asyncio.run per task.
corr: The mechanism is real but the impact description is wrong. Corrected claim: `embed_resume_task` (/Users/sanskar/dev/Latexy2/backend/app/workers/ats_worker.py:705-741) is the only Celery task that touches the module-global engine/session factory (`get_async_db_session`, /Users/sanskar/dev/Latexy2/backend/app/database/connection.py:73-83, globals at :16-17) from inside a per-task `asyncio.run()`, so pooled asyncpg connections outlive the loop they were created on. Reproduced with `backend/.venv/bin/python` against latexy-postgres:5434 using the real `connection.py`: sequential `asyncio.run(...)` calls fail on *alternating* invocations with `RuntimeError: ... got Future ... attached to a different loop`, raised from `pool_pre_ping` -> asyncpg `do_ping`. It is NOT "fails from the second task onward": the failing checkout invalidates the stale connection, so the very next run opens a fresh connection and succeeds, which then goes stale for the run after it (observed pattern ok/fail/ok/fail/... i.e. ~50% of first attempts). Because the task has `max_retries=2` / `default_retry_delay=60`, a retried attempt typically lands on a fresh connection and succeeds, so embeddings are usually stored eventually rather than lost. Real but smaller costs: ~half of embed attempts are wasted (including a wasted OpenAI embeddings call, since the DB connection is only acquired after the embedding is computed), up to 60s+ latency before the pgvector row lands, noisy error logs, and leaked/never-cleanly-closed asyncpg connections ("coroutine 'Connection._cancel' was never awaited"). Severity is low-to-medium, not medium-with-silent-data-loss. Fix is the same one the other workers already use (per-task `create_async_engine` + `await engine.dispose()` in `finally`, as in auto_save_worker.py:60-72/184, cover_letter_worker.py:314-336, interview_prep_worker.py:230-259, email_worker.py:53-100), or a `NullPool` engine for worker use.
evidence: `embed_resume_task` calls `asyncio.run(_async_embed_resume(...))`, which does `async with get_async_db_session() as db`. That helper uses the process-global `SessionLocal`/`engine` created once by `init_db()` and cached (`global engine, SessionLocal`), so the asyncpg connection pool created under the first task's event loop is reused after `asyncio.run` closes that loop. Every other Celery worker deliberately avoids this: auto_save_worker.py:60-72, cover_letter_worker.py:316-336 and interview_prep_worker.py:236-262 each build a throwaway `create_async_engine(...)` and `await engine.dispose()` in a `finally`.
repro: Save two different resumes in a row (each triggers submit_embed_resume) and inspect worker logs for the second task's DB error / check that resume_embeddings rows stop appearing.

title: Orchestrator delimiter state machine never flushes its residual buffer, silently truncating up to 14 characters of LaTeX
impact: If the model omits the closing `<<<END_LATEX>>>` marker (truncation at max_tokens, or format drift), the assembled LaTeX loses its tail — commonly the entire `\end{document}` — and the JSON fallback does not fire because `latex_parts` is non-empty. The compile stage then fails with a LaTeX error the user cannot explain, and the editor is left holding the truncated document.
fix: After the streaming loop, flush the remainder: if state is _IN_LATEX append `buf` to `latex_parts`, if _IN_CHANGES append to `changes_parts`; and warn when the end delimiter was never seen.
corr: The defect is real but only triggers when the stream ends while the state machine is still inside a hold-back state, i.e. when the model omits the closing marker (max_tokens truncation or format drift) — not on every response. In that case the final `buf` (exactly the last 14 chars for _IN_LATEX, since safe_len = len(buf) - 14) is discarded, and because latex_parts is non-empty the JSON fallback at orchestrator.py:471 is skipped, so the truncated document is compiled and pushed to the editor via llm.complete. The same missing post-loop flush also affects the _IN_CHANGES branch (orchestrator.py:452-461), dropping up to 16 chars of the changes JSON, which makes json.loads fail and silently produces changes_made = []. Fix: after `for chunk in stream:` exits, flush the residual buffer according to llm_state (append buf to latex_parts when llm_state == _IN_LATEX, to changes_parts when _IN_CHANGES) and log a warning that the closing delimiter was never seen. Severity low-to-medium rather than medium, since it requires the model to deviate from the requested output format.
evidence: In the `_IN_LATEX` branch the code intentionally holds back a partial-delimiter tail: `safe_len = len(buf) - len(_LE) + 1; if safe_len > 0: latex_parts.append(buf[:safe_len]); buf = buf[safe_len:]`. After `for chunk in stream:` exits, the code goes straight to `optimization_time = time.time() - start_time` and `optimized_latex = "".join(latex_parts).strip()` — `buf` is never appended. `_LE = "<<<END_LATEX>>>"` is 15 chars, so up to 14 trailing characters are dropped whenever the model ends the stream while still inside the LaTeX block. `\end{document}` is exactly 14 characters.
repro: Static-only; force the stream to end mid-LaTeX (e.g. set OPENAI_MAX_TOKENS low enough to truncate) and compare the published llm.complete content with the raw accumulated text.

title: Every streamed LLM token costs 6 sequential Redis round-trips, including a full job-state SETEX
impact: A single optimization streaming ~3000 deltas issues ~18000 blocking Redis commands from the worker thread, serialising token delivery behind Redis RTT and inflating optimization latency and Redis load for every concurrent job.
fix: Pipeline the writes inside publish_event (one `r.pipeline()` round-trip), and skip the `:state` SETEX for high-frequency non-status events such as `llm.token` / `log.line`.
corr: Confirmed with adjusted framing. publish_event does issue 6 sequential unpipelined Redis commands per event including a full state SETEX, and llm.token is published once per delta, so a ~3000-delta optimization issues ~18000 Redis commands where ~3000 would suffice. However the primary harm is Redis command-rate amplification (~6x per concurrent streaming job) plus a correctness bug, not optimization latency — the added worker-thread time is only ~1-3s against a 30-60s provider call. The correctness bug the finding omits: because llm.token payloads have no stage/percent, _update_state_snapshot rewrites latexy:job:{job_id}:state with stage="" and percent=0 on every token, so GET /jobs/{job_id}/state (job_routes.py:728) and public_api_routes.py:207 report percent 0 for the whole streaming phase, discarding the job.progress snapshot. Fix: wrap the writes in a single redis pipeline and skip _update_state_snapshot for llm.token (or preserve prior stage/percent when absent). Medium severity is appropriate given the correctness side effect.
evidence: `publish_event` unconditionally performs INCR + EXPIRE (`_next_sequence`), XADD + EXPIRE on the stream, PUBLISH, then `_update_state_snapshot` → SETEX. `status_from_event_type` has no entry for `llm.token`, so it falls through to `_STATUS_MAP.get(event_type, "processing")` and rewrites the whole snapshot for each token. llm_worker calls `publish_event(job_id, "llm.token", {"token": delta})` once per delta.
repro: Run an llm_optimization job and count commands with `redis-cli monitor | wc -l`, or observe `MONITOR` traffic during streaming.

title: `WorkspaceMember.role` (editor vs viewer) is validated on input but never checked by any handler
impact: The workspace role UI implies a permission difference between editor and viewer that does not exist; an operator changing a member to "viewer" gets no actual restriction. Currently low-impact because all mutating workspace endpoints happen to be owner-only, but it is a latent authz gap the moment a member-writable endpoint is added.
fix: Either enforce `member.role == "editor"` on member-writable endpoints, or remove the role field from the API surface until it is wired up.
corr: WorkspaceMember.role ("editor" vs "viewer") is validated on input, persisted, returned in MemberResponse, and settable via PATCH /workspaces/{id}/members/{uid}/role, but no backend code ever branches on it (unlike TenantMember.role, checked at tenant_routes.py:147 and :401). The frontend (frontend/src/app/workspaces/[workspaceId]/page.tsx:236,282) presents Editor/Viewer as a permission control, so the real defect is a misleading UI plus dead authorization metadata: viewers and editors have byte-identical capabilities. It is NOT a reachable authz gap today - every mutating workspace endpoint is _require_owner, and the two member-reachable writes (update/delete recruiter note, lines 627/664) are author-scoped while note creation (568) is owner-only, so no non-owner can ever reach them. Severity low is correct; the fix is either to enforce the role or to remove the UI control.
evidence: `grep -n 'role ==\|role !=' backend/app/api/workspace_routes.py` returns no matches. Every handler gates on either `_require_owner(ws, user_id)` (which compares `workspace.owner_id`) or `_require_member(ws, user_id, db)` (which only asserts a row exists). The role string is stored and returned in `MemberResponse` and settable via `PATCH /workspaces/{id}/members/{uid}/role`, but no code branches on it.
repro: static-only

title: Models declare index=True on FK columns that no migration ever created; three FK columns have no usable index
impact: Deleting a resume (ON DELETE CASCADE into recruiter_notes, career_analyses, workspace_resumes) forces a sequential scan of each child table; the same applies to user deletion via snippet_installs/snippet_upvotes. models.py is also misleading — it asserts indexes that exist in no deployed database, so anyone reasoning about query plans from the model file gets the wrong answer.
fix: Add a migration creating ix_recruiter_notes_resume_id, ix_career_analyses_resume_id and ix_workspace_resumes_resume_id (optionally the shared_by/invited_by/default_tenant_id/snippet user_id ones) with CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS so the DB matches the index=True declarations.
corr: Confirmed with narrowed scope. Two distinct issues are conflated. (1) Model/migration drift, affecting exactly two columns: models.py:723 and models.py:805 declare index=True on recruiter_notes.resume_id and career_analyses.resume_id, but migrations 0017 and 0021 only create composite indexes where resume_id is the trailing column, so these indexes exist in no deployed database. (2) Un-indexed FK columns with no such declaration (a design gap, not drift): workspace_resumes.resume_id and .shared_by (0016 creates no index on that table), snippet_installs.user_id, snippet_upvotes.user_id (both PK(snippet_id, user_id)), users.default_tenant_id, workspace_members.invited_by. Confirmed against the live DB at alembic head 0034 — the catalog query returns precisely these 8 columns, and neither 0030_add_missing_indexes.py nor 0034_db_integrity_and_indexes.py (a prior FK-index audit fix covering 12 other columns) addresses any of them. Impact holds but is modest: DELETE /resumes/{id} (backend/app/api/resume_routes.py:848) cascades into these child tables with a seq scan each; these are low-volume collaboration/marketplace tables and no read path is affected, so severity low is correct.
evidence: models.py declares `resume_id: ... ForeignKey("resumes.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), nullable=False, index=True` for both recruiter_notes and career_analyses, but 0017 only creates `idx_recruiter_notes_workspace_resume` on ['workspace_id','resume_id'] and 0021 only creates `ix_career_analyses_user_resume` on ['user_id','resume_id'] — resume_id is never the leading column. 0016 creates no index on workspace_resumes at all. A pg_constraint/pg_index catalog query for FK columns lacking a leading index returns: users.default_tenant_id, workspace_members.invited_by, workspace_resumes.shared_by, workspace_resumes.resume_id, recruiter_notes.resume_id, career_analyses.resume_id, snippet_installs.user_id, snippet_upvotes.user_id.
repro: static-only: run the pg_constraint/pg_index catalog query against a DB at head, or diff `\d recruiter_notes` against models.py:723.

title: Redundant duplicate index on session.token, plus a stale TODO claiming the index is missing
impact: Every session insert/update maintains two identical btrees on the same column for no benefit, and the code comment tells the next reader that session lookups are sequential scans when they have been index-backed since revision 0001.
fix: Drop idx_session_token in a follow-up migration (uq_session_token already serves the exact-match lookup) and delete the stale AUTH-003 TODO block.
corr: Redundant duplicate btree on session.token: 0001 creates uq_session_token (UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, backed by a unique btree) and 0032 additionally creates idx_session_token on the same column; head schema confirms both exist. Drop idx_session_token (and its downgrade line) since the unique constraint already serves equality lookups. Separately, the TODO(AUTH-003) comment in auth_middleware.py:46-49 is stale and should be removed or rewritten — it is not false (it hedges "sequential scan or btree on the raw token value") and its real ask was a hashed/expression index, which was never implemented; the plain btree it suggests as an alternative has existed since 0001. Impact is limited to negligible write amplification on a small table plus reader confusion — no correctness or performance defect.
evidence: 0001 already created `sa.UniqueConstraint("token", name="uq_session_token")`, which Postgres backs with a unique btree. 0032 then adds `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_session_token ON session (token)`. `\d session` at head shows both `idx_session_token btree (token)` and `uq_session_token UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, btree (token)`. auth_middleware.py still states: `# TODO(AUTH-003): token column should have a hashed index ... Currently relies on a full sequential scan or btree on the raw token value. Add a schema migration to create the index before this table grows large.`

title: No React error boundary is mounted anywhere despite ErrorBoundary.tsx existing; three other components are orphaned
impact: Any uncaught render exception in the heavy client pages (Monaco editor, PDF preview, Yjs collab binding) produces Next.js's default error screen or a blank page with no recovery affordance, instead of the styled fallback already sitting in the repo.
fix: Add `frontend/src/app/error.tsx` (and `global-error.tsx`) wired to the existing `ErrorBoundary` fallback UI, or wrap the workspace layout in `<ErrorBoundary>`; delete the two orphaned job/JD components or wire them where the docs claim they are reused.
corr: Downgrade to informational/dead-code cleanup, and split into two items. (1) No React error boundary is mounted: ErrorBoundary.tsx exists but is never imported, and no error.tsx/global-error.tsx exists in any app-router segment, so uncaught render errors fall through to Next 14's built-in fallback (dev overlay, or the prod "Application error: a client-side exception has occurred" page) rather than the styled fallback with a reset button already in the repo. This is a missing-polish/resilience gap, not a crash-to-blank-page bug, and the fix is adding error.tsx to heavy segments (workspace/[resumeId]/edit, optimize) or wrapping in layout.tsx. (2) Separately, ErrorBoundary.tsx, JobStatusTracker.tsx, and JobDescriptionInput.tsx are unreferenced dead code; JobDescriptionInput.tsx in particular is a prototype with a hardcoded 30-line SAMPLE_JOB_DESCRIPTION that was superseded by the inline JD textarea in workspace/[resumeId]/optimize/page.tsx, so FEATURES.md 2.1's "reuses JD component from optimize page" is already satisfied and no feature is missing.
evidence: `rg -n 'ErrorBoundary' frontend/src --glob '!components/ErrorBoundary.tsx'` returns nothing, and `find frontend/src/app -name 'error.tsx' -o -name 'global-error.tsx'` returns nothing — neither the custom boundary nor Next.js App Router's `error.tsx` convention exists in any route segment. `JobStatusTracker.tsx` and `JobDescriptionInput.tsx` are also imported by zero files, even though FEATURES.md 2.1 / P0 Feature 4F describe "reuses JD component from optimize page".

title: WebSocket job-ownership check fails open on Redis errors and missing metadata
impact: During a Redis hiccup, any connection — including anonymous ones — can subscribe to and `cancel` any job id it knows or guesses, cancelling other users' in-flight work. The behaviour is also inconsistent with the REST surface, so the same job id is 404 over HTTP and readable over WS.
fix: Fail closed in both branches (deny on lookup error and on missing meta), matching the REST ownership check.
corr: `_job_ws_access_ok` (backend/app/api/ws_routes.py:184-200) fails open in two branches (`except Exception -> True`, `not meta_raw -> True`), diverging from the REST endpoints which 404/403. The Redis-error branch is mostly inert because the subsequent subscribe/cancel operations use the same Redis client and would fail too, and mainstream job types always write `latexy:job:{id}:meta` before enqueue so a live job is never meta-less. The one genuinely reachable case is job types that never write meta: `/api/v1/interview` (backend/app/api/interview_routes.py:97) enqueues a job with no meta record, while backend/app/workers/interview_prep_worker.py publishes its events and honors `is_cancelled`. An unauthenticated WS connection that *knows* such a job id can therefore replay its events and cancel it. Job ids are uuid4 and WS is rate limited to 20 msg/s, so ids cannot be guessed — the id must leak first. Severity low is appropriate; the fix is to default-deny on both branches (and/or write job meta for every job type, e.g. by actually using the dead `store_job_meta` helper in backend/app/workers/event_publisher.py:183).
evidence: `_job_ws_access_ok` returns True in the `except Exception` branch (`logger.debug(...); return True`) and again when meta is absent (`if not meta_raw: return True`). The equivalent REST endpoint does the opposite: `if not meta_raw: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Job not found")`.
repro: Static-only: block Redis GET (or let meta TTL expire while the stream still exists) and subscribe/cancel with an arbitrary job id.

title: ?next= redirect parameter is generated but never honoured after sign-in
impact: A user who is bounced to login while trying to upgrade (or to create a developer key) is dropped on /workspace after authenticating and must re-navigate and re-do the action. The `next` parameter is dead.
fix: Read `next` from `useSearchParams()` in the login page, validate it is a relative path, and use it for both `window.location.href` and the social `callbackURL`.
corr: Confirmed as a real low-severity defect, with two adjustments: (1) the billing producer lines are frontend/src/app/billing/page.tsx:188 and :446, not :181; (2) the impact is limited to a UX detour — the user lands authenticated on /workspace and must manually re-navigate to Billing/Developer and redo the click. There is no security implication (and, conversely, no open-redirect risk, since the untrusted `next` value is never used as a redirect target). Fix requires reading useSearchParams() in SignInForm (wrapped in Suspense) and threading the value into both window.location.href and the social callbackURL, with an allowlist/same-origin check on the value.
evidence: Billing does `router.push('/login?next=/billing')` and Developer does `router.push('/login?next=/developer')`, but `SignInForm` hardcodes `window.location.href = '/workspace'` on success and never reads `useSearchParams()`; the social helpers are also fixed: `authClient.signIn.social({ provider, callbackURL: '/workspace' })`. `/login/page.tsx` does not read or forward the query param either.
repro: Sign out, open /billing, click a paid plan → redirected to /login?next=/billing → sign in → you land on /workspace.

title: Proxy route PUT /api/byok/api-keys/[keyId] forwards to a backend route that does not exist
impact: No user impact today (unreachable), but the route silently converts any future caller's 405 into a generic 500 `{success:false,error:'Failed to update API key'}` because non-404 failures are re-thrown into the catch-all.
fix: Delete the PUT handler, or add a matching `PATCH/PUT /byok/api-keys/{key_id}` endpoint on the backend.
corr: Accurate but should be reclassified as informational dead-code cleanup, not a defect. The PUT handler in frontend/src/app/api/byok/api-keys/[keyId]/route.ts (lines 41-79) forwards to a path where the backend only registers POST/GET/DELETE, so it would return 405 -> proxy 500. It has no callers (APIKeyManager.tsx uses only GET/POST/DELETE) and no functional, security, or data impact. The "405 masked as 500" behaviour is the standard pattern in all 7 of these proxy handlers (including the DELETE in the same file), so it is not unique to this route. Fix is simply to delete the unused PUT export (or add the missing backend PUT if key rotation is intended).
evidence: The proxy defines `PUT` and forwards to `${BACKEND_URL}/byok/api-keys/${keyId}`. The byok router only declares `POST /api-keys`, `GET /api-keys` and `DELETE /api-keys/{key_id}` — there is no PUT/PATCH on that path, so FastAPI answers 405. No frontend code calls it (`APIKeyManager` only uses GET/POST/DELETE).
repro: `curl -X PUT http://localhost:5180/api/byok/api-keys/<id> -d '{}' -H 'content-type: application/json'` → 500.

title: docker-compose.prod.yml nginx healthcheck probes port 80 /health, which only ever returns a 301 redirect
impact: The nginx container reports unhealthy forever (busybox wget follows the redirect to https://localhost with an untrusted/self-signed cert), so orchestration and dashboards cannot distinguish a genuinely broken proxy from this false negative.
fix: Add a plain `location /health { return 200 "healthy\n"; }` to the port-80 server block (before the redirect), or change the healthcheck to `wget --no-check-certificate -q -O- https://localhost/health`.
corr: Finding confirmed, with the mechanism refined: the probe fails before TLS is even reached because busybox wget resolves `localhost` to `::1` while nginx.conf's `listen 80;` binds IPv4 only (verified: "Connecting to localhost ([::1]:80) ... Connection refused"). When forced to IPv4, it then fails exactly as claimed on the 301 to https with `certificate verify failed` from ssl_client (Alpine's busybox wget does validate certs via openssl). Fix is either adding `location /health { return 200 "healthy\n"; }` to the port-80 server block (also lets it serve as a plain HTTP LB probe) or changing the healthcheck to `wget --no-check-certificate --spider https://127.0.0.1/health`. Impact should be stated as monitoring-signal-only: no compose service uses `condition: service_healthy` on nginx and scripts/deploy/deploy.sh does not read container health, so nothing functional breaks.
evidence: Compose healthcheck: `test: ["CMD","wget","--no-verbose","--tries=1","--spider","http://localhost:80/health"]`. In nginx.conf the port-80 server block is `server { listen 80; server_name _; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; }` — the only `location /health { return 200 "healthy\n"; }` lives in the 443 TLS server, behind a self-signed cert mounted from ./nginx/ssl.
repro: docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up nginx; docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <nginx> → unhealthy.

title: `POST /compile` and `POST /public/compile` are Docker-only and cannot work in the Docker deployment; the failure path also leaks temp dirs
impact: Two publicly documented compile endpoints (including the anonymous trial one, which burns a trial use before compiling) always fail with a raw `[Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'docker'` message. Harmless today only because the frontend routes everything through `/jobs/submit`. Dead helper invites future divergence from the real worker.
fix: Either delete `/compile`, `/public/compile`, `run_latex_subprocess` and `LaTeXService.compile_latex`, or make them delegate to `submit_latex_compilation`; move the temp-dir cleanup into a `finally` regardless of success.
corr: `LaTeXService.compile_latex` (backend/app/services/latex_service.py:117-131) is Docker-CLI-only with no local-pdflatex fallback, so in the fully containerized backend deployment (no docker CLI in backend/Dockerfile, no /var/run/docker.sock mount anywhere) both `POST /compile` (auth-required) and `POST /public/compile` (anonymous, trial-metered) return HTTP 200 with success=False and message "Compilation error: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'docker'". /public/compile consumes a trial use before that failure. Because cleanup is scheduled only under `if result.success`, the failure path orphans {TEMP_DIR}/{job_id}/resume.tex until the beat sweep, which uses max_age_hours=24 (not 30 min). Impact is low: the frontend routes everything through /jobs/submit, the documented developer endpoint is /api/v1/compile (which correctly queues via submit_latex_compilation and the worker's docker/local fallback), and the path works in hybrid dev where a host docker CLI exists. Separately confirmed: `run_latex_subprocess` (latex_service.py:223) is dead code whose docstring falsely claims latex_worker.py and orchestrator.py call it; the error message leaks no user data.
evidence: `LaTeXService.compile_latex` hardcodes `docker_cmd = ["docker", "run", "--rm", ...]` with no local-binary fallback (unlike `latex_worker`, which checks `shutil.which("docker")`). Inside the backend container there is no docker CLI, so `create_subprocess_exec` raises `FileNotFoundError`, caught by `except Exception as e: return CompilationResponse(success=False, ..., message=f"Compilation error: {str(e)}")` — a 200 response claiming failure. Both endpoints then only schedule cleanup on success: `if result.success: asyncio.create_task(latex_service.cleanup_temp_files_delayed(job_dir, ...))`, so the failure path leaves `{TEMP_DIR}/{job_id}/resume.tex` (full resume content) behind for the 30-minute beat sweep. Separately, `run_latex_subprocess` (latex_service.py:223) documents itself as "used by both latex_worker.py and orchestrator.py" but `grep run_latex_subprocess backend/` matches only its own definition — it is dead code, and its `for raw_line in proc.stdout` loop is also the only compile path with no `-halt-on-error`.
repro: `curl -F 'device_fingerprint=x' -F 'latex_content=...' http://localhost:8030/api/v1/public/compile` inside the docker-compose stack.

title: /health reports `latex_available: true` whenever the docker CLI exists, even with no daemon or image
impact: An operator's readiness dashboard reports `status: "healthy", latex_available: true` on a host where the Docker daemon is stopped or the texlive image was never pulled, while every compile fails. Startup logging in main.py is misleading for the same reason.
fix: Have `is_available()` call `docker image inspect` (or reuse `latex_service.check_latex_installation()`) and re-evaluate on each health call rather than caching at import.
corr: Corrected claim (informational/cosmetic, severity low or lower): LaTeXCompiler._check_docker_available (backend/app/services/latex_compiler.py:31-43) only verifies the docker CLI exists, and is_available() returns True immediately when use_docker is set without inspecting the daemon or the texlive image. Because the singleton is constructed at import (line 272), the result is cached for the process lifetime. Consequently /health's informational latex_available field (backend/app/api/routes.py:239) and the startup log in backend/app/main.py:71-79 can claim LaTeX is available on a host where the docker daemon is stopped or the image was never pulled. This is reporting-only: latex_compiler is not used by any compile path (real compiles use LaTeXService.compile_latex), /health always returns HTTP 200, and the orchestrator readiness gate /readyz (routes.py:286-313) checks only DB/Redis, so no traffic gating or compile decision is affected. The condition is also not reachable in the shipped container image (backend/Dockerfile installs texlive and has no docker CLI). Fix: reuse LaTeXService.check_latex_installation (which adds `docker image inspect settings.LATEX_DOCKER_IMAGE`) and re-evaluate per request with a short TTL cache. Related nit: LaTeXCompiler.__init__ hardcodes docker_image="texlive/texlive:latest" instead of settings.LATEX_DOCKER_IMAGE.
evidence: `_check_docker_available` returns `subprocess.run(["docker", "--version"]).returncode == 0` — which succeeds with no daemon running — and `is_available()` short-circuits: `if self.use_docker: return True` without ever inspecting the image. The correct check exists but is unused by the health endpoint: `LaTeXService.check_latex_installation` additionally runs `docker image inspect settings.LATEX_DOCKER_IMAGE`. The values are also computed once at import (`latex_compiler = LaTeXCompiler()`), so the health answer never changes for the process lifetime.
repro: Stop the Docker daemon on a host that has the docker CLI, start the backend, `GET /api/v1/health` → healthy.

title: llm_worker and cover_letter_worker stream the raw delimiter scaffold to the editor, contradicting the documented behaviour
impact: During cover-letter generation and llm_optimization jobs the user watches `<<<LATEX>>>` and a trailing JSON array appear inside the editor until `llm.complete` replaces the buffer; if `llm.complete` is missed (reconnect) the scaffold is what stays on screen and, for cover letters, what the user may save.
fix: Reuse the orchestrator's delimiter state machine (extract it into a shared helper) in llm_worker and cover_letter_worker, or strip markers client-side before rendering.
corr: cover_letter_worker.py:194 streams raw LLM deltas without the delimiter filtering the orchestrator applies, so the cover-letter editor transiently displays the literal `<<<LATEX>>>` marker (and any pre-delimiter prose) until `llm.complete` swaps in the parsed body. Cosmetic only: there is no CHANGES/JSON scaffold in the cover-letter prompt, the DB copy is always the regex-extracted LaTeX, missed events are replayed via `last_event_id`, and the llm_worker path is never wired to a Monaco editor in the UI. Severity: informational/nit, not a correctness bug.
evidence: Both workers publish every raw delta: `publish_event(job_id, "llm.token", {"token": delta})` with no delimiter filtering, so `<<<LATEX>>>`, `<<<END_LATEX>>>`, `<<<CHANGES>>>` and the JSON change list are streamed verbatim. The reducer appends them (`case 'llm.token': streamingLatex: state.streamingLatex + event.token`) and the cover-letter page pipes that straight into Monaco: `if (!stream.streamingLatex || !editorRef.current) return; editorRef.current.setValue(stream.streamingLatex)`. Only the orchestrator filters, and its module docstring claims globally "only LaTeX tokens published via llm.token (JSON scaffold never reaches editor)".
repro: Run a cover-letter generation job with the editor open and watch the streamed text.
